I'm running into a familiar issue with a website I'm building. I ask for more information about different things my "client" wants on their site, but I find that communication is only flowing in one direction. My question for you other devs, how long do you wait for an answer from someone before you throw up your hands and say, "forget it"?

A previous situation for a frame of reference: A few years ago, I was asked to design (from scratch) the website for our local soccer association. It took two weeks to get the login information for the website from the director of the association. Then, once I was in and making changes, weeks went by without a peep from anyone when I would send multiple emails asking for input and more details. All of the work I was doing was pro bono. So, after about a month of no communication back to me, I gave up on it and dropped it. I emailed to let the director know, and never got a response to that, either.

Today's situation: I'm working on the site for our church. Some of the same problems are cropping up again. I have a few people who just refuse to tell me what I need to know. For instance, the pre-k education director will not send me a curriculum or general information so that I can add it to the site for parents of potential students. It's not as if I'm getting told to wait or that she doesn't want to add it. I'm literally getting nothing. On one of my vacation days last year, I went to the church offices and did some basic IT for them. I made sure that EVERYONE'S email was working on their device of choice--a couple of android phones and Windows PCs. So, I know for a fact that she has received the requests. Still, I've gotten nothing. So, I have a choice: Throw my hands up in the air or get the pastor involved. (The second option is kind of like getting CEO buy-in before designing/changing a system in the IT world.)

So, other devs out there, given the vague description here, what would you do?

Note: The people in the two examples are different. I just wanted to explain how I handled a previous, somewhat similar situation.
[LIFE] How long until you drop a project from non-responsive "clients"? Do you use an alternate method for getting information?
They expect you to be the expert, plus a mind reader. I imagine them sitting covered in sweat, wondering why you expect them to think.

I think it even goes beyond that. They also tend to expect full service website building. Not only do I need to design and code the site, I also need to go to events to take pictures that will end up on the site...

Late to the party, but here we go. In most of the chance that I had, the user does not know what they want. And second, you won't get any respond from e-mail. Call them, make appointment, ask them in person.

However, chance is everything that have been discussed can be changed at one point by client. Clarify everything upfront in contract (if any), that the requirement will be discussed in (#) times of meeting. Any change after that will resulting in additional charge. After each meeting, write them up in memo. Demand down payment after proposal agreement, before you do any design.

During the development, you may meet with small decision that need respond from client. Send them mail about it. Ask question, and at the same time describe what action that you will take, and state that if no reply then the action will be taken.

I don't know whether involving the pastor will bring you any good response or not (I don't know the exact situation). Who make the request for it? Who is in charge for it? However if the pre-k education director is the one who made request and in charge for it, just throw your hands up. Chances are, if she does not respond your e-mail, she doesn't regard the website important. Thus it's high probable that your website won't be used at all.

TL;DR: in business IT, the negotiation, requirement gathering and communication activities outnumber the effort required for development. It's different with product development (ex: AI, robot, embedded software).

You're not late to the party at all. Thank you for responding.
